title: Ketef Hinnom silver amulet KH2 (the priestly blessing), Israel Museum
source: Ketef Hinnom amulet KH2, Israel Museum: photograph via Wikimedia Commons + text, transliteration and English from English Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0)
description: The smaller Ketef Hinnom silver amulet (about 600 BCE), whose twelve surviving lines include the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24-26, with its text, transliteration and translation and a photograph of the unrolled amulet.
introduction:
The Ketef Hinnom amulets are two tiny rolled strips of silver found in 1979 by Gabriel Barkay in a burial cave at Ketef Hinnom, on the slope above the Hinnom valley in Jerusalem. They date from the late 7th or early 6th century BCE, before the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem, and were worn as amulets. Unrolled and read, both carry words of the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24-26, 'The LORD bless thee, and keep thee: The LORD make his face shine upon thee', which makes them the oldest surviving text that is also found in the Old Testament. They are in the Israel Museum, Jerusalem.

This entry gives the smaller amulet, KH2 (about 11 by 39 mm): its twelve preserved lines in Hebrew letters, a transliteration and an English rendering, all from Wikipedia. Lines 5-12 contain the blessing. The top of the strip is lost. The larger amulet, KH1, is not included here because no openly licensed original-language text of it was available.
translator_notes: The English renders word-divisions across line ends as the amulet has them ('h/sh-', 'YH-/-[W]H', 'g-/-rant', 'p-/-[ea]ce'); a slash gives two possible readings.
Lines 5-12 correspond to Numbers 6:24-25 and the last words of 6:26: 'The LORD bless thee, and keep thee: The LORD make his face shine upon thee ... and give thee peace' (KJV).
In lines 5 and 12 the square brackets of the Hebrew-letter text are placed as in Wikipedia's transliteration of the same lines; the Wikipedia markup has them displaced.
Text, transliteration and English from English Wikipedia, 'Ketef Hinnom scrolls', revision 1378179986 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ketef_Hinnom_scrolls), under CC BY-SA 4.0.

translation.scan_note: The twelve preserved lines are on the one inscribed side of the unrolled silver strip, which the photograph shows whole (checked on the image: the strip mounted on a plate, broken at the top, with fine scratched letters running across its width; the letters are very small and faint, the strip being about 11 mm wide, and the detached pieces at the bottom come from the lower end). Lines are numbered from the top of the preserved text as in Wikipedia. Square brackets are restorations, not visible on the silver.
